🍎 Lesson plan · 🌍 AI in your world · Lesson 15

Lesson plan: Plan Your Own AI Project

From an idea to a working model: choosing a problem, collecting data, testing honestly and thinking about the people it affects.

By the end of the lesson, students can

  • decide whether a problem needs AI or a simple rule;
  • plan the data for a project: varied examples of every answer, with correct labels, and a test set;
  • explain why one accuracy score isn't enough, and how to be honest with users about a model's limits.

Warm-up

Think of a small problem at school or at home that annoys you. Could a computer help? Would it need to learn, or just follow a rule?

Write a few problems on the board and sort them together into “a rule is enough” and “it would need examples”. Keep the list for the extension task.

Reading

Students read the lesson “Plan Your Own AI Project”. Students look for when AI is worth using, what makes good training examples, and why accuracy can fool you.

Activity: Mini-lab “Project planner”

  1. Students open the mini-lab in lesson 15 and read the project: a leaf-health app.
  2. For each of the four decisions, they discuss the options in pairs before choosing.
  3. They read the feedback, go back to change any choice marked in orange, and reach the final plan.
  4. They fill in the worksheet's table with the strong choice for each step, and one sentence on why.

For students who finish early

Fast finishers pick a problem from the warm-up that needs examples, and write a one-page plan with the same four decisions: data, labels, testing, and what users are told.

Discussion questions

  • A model is right 95% of the time. Is that good enough for sorting recycling? For checking medicine doses? Why the difference?
  • Which is worse for a leaf-health app: calling a sick leaf healthy, or a healthy leaf sick?
  • Why might a project that works well at home fail in a real school?
  • Should every AI app say clearly that it is AI? Why?

Exit ticket

In one sentence, explain why a model that always answers “healthy” could still score 95%.

Quick check. 95 of your 100 test leaves are healthy. A model that always answers “healthy” scores 95%. What does this show?
Right answer: Accuracy alone can hide that a model is useless for what matters

Easier and harder

Easier. Run the mini-lab together on the projector, voting on each decision with hands up, and reading each piece of feedback aloud.

Harder. Students train a real model on their own photos with a free tool such as Teachable Machine, keep some photos aside as a test set, and report the results and the mistakes.
